column2: All this world that is seen, moving and unmoving, perishes at the end of the cosmic age like a dream in deep sleep.
Truth, "Self," "Supreme Brahman," "Reality" and the like are names imagined by the wise for the sake of usage for that great one.
As the meaning of the word "bracelet" is not apart from gold, so the meaning of the word "world" is not apart from the supreme.
By that, this splendor of magic is spread in the world; the bondage is said to be the existence of the seer within the seen.
The seer is bound by the seen and is freed when the seen is absent; the seen is said to be creation itself in the form "world," "I" and the like.
By the mind alone the splendor of magic is spread in the world; as long as this arises, there is no liberation.
The universe is spread by Brahma, the self-born, by the mind alone; therefore the universe that is seen is made of mind.
The mind has no real form either outside or in the heart; that by which an object appears is called mind.
Know the mind to be intention; the intention does not exist apart; wherever there is intention, understand that there is mind.
Intention and mind are never different for anyone; when what is born of intention dissolves, one's own nature remains.
When the confusion of the seen in the form "I," "you," "world" and the like is quieted, there will be such aloneness when the seen reaches its being.
At the great dissolution, when all the seen reaches non-being, at the beginning of creation only the quiet remains.
There is a luminous, unsetting, unborn, faultless god, ever the maker of all, all — declared the Supreme Self.
From where words turn back, who is known by the liberated, whose names like "Self" are imagined and not natural.
Mind-space, consciousness-space, and space as the third; know the consciousness-space, great sage, to be emptier than the other two.
When consciousness passes from place to place, the interval between is, in a moment, the consciousness-space; know that, best of sages.
If you attain in it the state of all intentions cast away, then without doubt you will reach the quiet state that is the Self of all.
That which is pregnant with the rise of the flavor of nobility, beauty and dispassion, and streams bliss, is called samadhi.
The delight that arises forcibly when attachment, hatred and the like are thinned by the knowledge of the impossibility of the seen is called samadhi.
The knowledge of the impossibility of the seen is knowledge itself, the known being of the nature of consciousness; that alone is aloneness; everything else is false.
A mad Airavata is tied in the hollow of a mustard seed; a mosquito wages war with herds of lions in a pollen grain.
Meru is placed in the eye of a lotus and swallowed by a bee's child; Nidagha, know the world to be of such a nature, deluded.
The mind alone is the world, defiled by disease and other afflictions; that same mind, freed from them, is the end of becoming.
The embodied one, being contemplated by the mind, takes on a body; freed from the impression of body, he is not tainted by the body's properties.
Within, one turns an age into a moment and brings a moment to an age; "the world is the play of the mind" — this is my settled conviction.
One who has not turned away from wrongdoing, who is not peaceful, not concentrated, nor of unpeaceful mind, cannot attain this even by knowledge.
Having known that Brahman-bliss, without duality, without qualities, true mass of consciousness, as the form of one's own self, one never fears.
The highest of the high, the greatest of the great, eternal and auspicious, made of the radiance of his own nature, the ancient seer, the eternal Person, Lord of all, worshipped by all gods.
I am Brahman is the sure cause of liberation for the great-souled. Two words serve for bondage and liberation: "not mine" and "mine." By "mine" a creature is bound; by "not mine" he is freed.
In the forms of individual and Lord, sentient and insentient — creation, from seeing to entering, is imagined by the Lord; the world, from waking to liberation, is imagined by the individual.
Those from Trinaciketa to the Yoga schools rely on the illusion of the Lord; those from Lokayata to Samkhya rely on the illusion of the individual.
Therefore seekers of liberation should not fix their mind on theories of individual and Lord; rather the truth of Brahman should be inquired into steadily.
He who sees all without distinction through the connection with consciousness is truly the knower; he is Shiva, he is Hari, he is Brahma.
Giving up of objects is hard to obtain; vision of truth is hard to obtain; the natural state is hard to obtain without the grace of a true teacher.
For the yogi in whom the power of knowledge has risen and who has given up all actions, the natural state arises of itself.
When a man perceives even a slight difference between this and himself, then fear arises for him; there is no doubt.
The eye of knowledge beholds the all-pervading being-consciousness-bliss; the eye of ignorance does not see the shining sun, like the blind.
Consciousness alone is that Brahman, having the mark of true consciousness; thus by knowing Brahman alone a mortal becomes immortal.
The knot of the heart is cut, all doubts are severed, and his actions are exhausted, when that Highest and Lowest is seen.
Abandoning the notion of non-Self, being unaffected in the world's stay, remain within in one-pointedness, devoted to pure awareness alone.
In the desert the water is all just desert; likewise these three worlds are all pure consciousness by one's own inquiry.
He who abandons the notion of the indicated and the unindicated and stays as the Self alone is Shiva himself, the best of the knowers of Brahman.
The substratum, without comparison, beyond speech and mind, eternal, all-pervading, omnipresent, very subtle, imperishable.
The mind and the world are the play of the Great Lord who has all power; by restraint and non-restraint the world goes to peace.
For the cure of the mind's disease I tell you the means: giving up whatever object is dear to oneself, one attains liberation.
Fie on that worm of a man for whom it is difficult — what lies in his own power, alone beneficial, the knowledge of giving up one's wishes.
Without the mere quieting of the mind, accomplishable by one's own effort alone, in the form of giving up one's wishes, there is no auspicious goal.
When this mind is cut by the sword of non-intention, then everything becomes all-pervading, quiet Brahman.
Be free by contemplation, free by supreme intellect; hold the Self unagitated; the mind that is swallowed is the state of consciousness.
Relying on supreme effort, bringing the mind to mindlessness, by meditation in the heart-space, in consciousness, with the stream of the wheel of consciousness.
Kill the mind without fear; enemies do not bind you.
This I am, this is that of mine — the mind is merely this much; by merely not contemplating it, it dissolves as by a sickle.
As a mass of scattered clouds is blown away in autumn in the sky, so the mind is blown away within by the wind of the cosmic age.
Let the winds of the end of the age blow, let the oceans become one, let the twelve suns burn; for the mindless there is no harm.
In the empire of non-intention, attainable by non-intention alone, which gives all accomplishments, stay firm in that state.
A mind without restlessness is not seen anywhere; restlessness is the mind's property, as heat is of fire.
This restless power of vibration is established in the nature of mind; know it as the mental power, of the nature of the world's pageant.
That which is without restlessness is called the mind's immortality; that alone in the conclusion of the scriptures is called austerity and liberation.
Its restlessness is this ignorance of the nature of impressions; destroy it by inquiry, called by the other name of impression.
By human effort and endeavor, whatever state the mind is joined to, having reached that state, be free of conceptions, O sinless one.
Therefore relying on effort, overcoming the mind with mind, taking hold of the sorrowless state, be fearless and steady.
Only the mind is able in firmly restraining the mind, as without a king one is powerless in the work of restraining a king.
For those seized by the crocodile of craving, falling into the ocean of the world, carried far by whirlpools, one's own mind alone is the boat.
Cutting the noose, the supreme bondage, with the mind alone, carry yourself across becoming; he is not carried across by another.
Whichever impression arises that is called mind, perfumed within, the wise should avoid each; then ignorance will be destroyed.
Giving up the sole impression of enjoyment, give up the impression of difference; then, abandoning being and non-being, be free of conceptions and happy.
This alone is the destruction of mind and of ignorance: that whatever is perceived, one avoids reliance on it.
Non-reliance alone is liberation; reliance and taking hold is sorrow.
Ignorance, though non-existent, is seen among those whose insight is destroyed; it has form accepted by name alone; how could it exist for one of right insight?
So long it swings the embodied one, together with himself, on the cliffs of the world, thick with thorns of sorrow.
As long as the destroyer of this ignorance has not arisen — the desire to see the Self oneself that destroys delusion.
For those who look beyond it, the destruction of this self-ignorance is born; when the all-pervading knowledge is seen, it dissolves by itself.
This ignorance is mere desire; its destruction is called liberation; and it is accomplished by non-intention alone, O sage.
In the sky of the mind, when the night of impressions wanes, even a little, the darkness thins by the shining of the sun of consciousness.
That principle of consciousness, free of attachment to the perceived and commonly all-pervading, indescribable — that is the Self, the Supreme Lord.
All this indeed is Brahman, the eternal mass of consciousness, unbroken; there is no other imagination called mind at all.
Nothing here in the three worlds is born or dies; nor does the being of the modifications of existence exist anywhere.
Only the alone, shining as alone, common to all, unbroken, free of attachment to the perceived — mere consciousness exists here.
In that eternal, extended, pure, mere consciousness, undisturbed, quiet, with the enjoyment of peace, changeless, the Self of consciousness.

That which runs, imagining by itself what accords with its nature — conscious perceived, itself unfading — is called mind by thinking. So this, established by intention, is destroyed by intention alone.
By the firm intention "I am not Brahman," the mind is bound; by the firm intention "all is Brahman," the mind is freed.
I am thin, I am bound by sorrow, I have hands and feet — by acting according to such notions one is bound.
I am not sorrowful, the body is not mine; what bondage exists in the Self? — by acting according to such notions one is freed.
I am not flesh and bones; I am other than the body, the supreme — he who is thus settled within, with ignorance wasted, is freed.

This ignorance is imagined, from the notion of Self in the non-Self. Relying on supreme effort, with effort and supreme intellect, giving up the wish for enjoyment far away, be free of conceptions and happy.
My son, my wealth, I am he, this is mine — thus an impression prances about like a magic show.
Do not be ignorant; be knowing; abandon the contemplation of the world; why do you weep like the ignorant, by the notion of Self in the non-Self?
What is this body of yours, dull, mute, made of flesh, impure, for whose sake you are helplessly overcome by pleasure and pain?
Oh, how strange that men have forgotten the Brahman that is truth! While you stand in your tasks, let there be no coloring of attachment.
Oh, how strange that mountains are bound by threads from a lotus! By that knowledge which does not exist, the world is laid waste.
This three-world has become like a thunderbolt, a mere blade of grass.
Thus the Upanishad.
Ribhu said: Now I shall tell you the other; listen, dear one, as it is. The ground of ignorance has seven stages, and the ground of knowledge also seven stages.
Countless other stages arise in these two otherwise. Abiding in one's own nature is liberation; falling from it is the perception of "I-ness."
Those in whom feelings like attachment and hatred do not move away from the awareness of pure mere being, one's own nature — in them ignorance cannot arise.
The falling away from one's own nature, the immersion of consciousness in objects — no other delusion than this has been or will be.
The mind goes from object to object; the state in the middle, with thinking destroyed, is called abiding in one's own nature.
That state of rock-like stillness, with all intentions quieted, free of waking and sleep, is the supreme abiding in one's own nature.
When the portion of ego is destroyed and quieted, the unmoving, non-inert state of mind, free of the vibration of difference, which moves — that is declared to be one's own nature.
The seed-waking, then waking, great waking, likewise waking-dream, then dream, dream-waking, and deep sleep.
